rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.2 and Fig. 2 report the authors' own SDrOP model runs for a baseline Kenyan farm case (Table 1); Section 4 reports a seven-day prototype experiment in Cambridge, MA with measured solar, battery, pump and pressure data (Figs. 5-9).
rows.notes: The 18-74% lifetime cost saving and 31-66% reliability gain quoted in the passage come solely from the economic analysis in Section 2.2: a simulation of cost-optimised SPDI designs (SDrOP model, SPM scheduling) for a hypothetical 2 ha tomato farm in Nyeri, Kenya at three well depths, benchmarked against designs from the Grundfos sizing tool operated with SSO. This is a model run on design data; its outputs (life cycle cost, season irrigation reliability) were never compared with measurements from the real system, and the authors state that further validation is needed to show how the economic results change for different conditions. Note also that most of the saving is attributable to the SDrOP design optimisation versus the Grundfos tool rather than to the scheduling approach itself (SPM alone gave +3%, -25%, -18% versus optimised SSO). The seven-day prototype experiment did produce measured results (up to 46% higher solar irrigation reliability on high-demand days, 0.3 kWh vs 1.8 kWh battery buffer, 6-16% pumping energy savings from Level 1), but the comparison was against a simulated SSO reference, no crops were grown, no lifetime cost was measured, and the numbers differ from those in the passage. Because the specific claimed effect rests on an unvalidated simulation, Q2 is answered no and Q3-Q9 follow as no. Had the simulation counted, the study would still have been single-site for the simulation (three well depths of one farm case, not three regions), reported no dispersion measures for the cost/reliability figures, and stated limitations only for the prototype (small scale, seven days, no crops, LFP battery) and a general need for further economic validation.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references, with appendices). The study is a design-and-prototype paper: the economic figures cited in the passage are purely simulated; the experimental component is a small-scale, seven-day prototype without crops and with a simulated typical-practice benchmark.
